_comment: The design questions: requirements that ask how the system is built, which the owner knows and no scanner reaches. Answered in stackvet.toml's [design] section as yes, no, not-sure, or planned (decided, not built yet), with `where` naming the file that does it, or will. An answer of yes is *attested by the owner* — the weakest tier there is, and never evidence that the control is really there, because the owner asserting a property is not the property. An answer of no is a finding: the owner has said the control is missing. `where` pointing at a file that is not in the app is a finding too, because a stale pointer is worse than none. Each question's words (`asks`, the citation) are read against its requirement by crates/sv-check/tests/design.rs, the same way the security notes are; `plain` is the same question in one sentence a person who is not a programmer can answer, asked first (backlog 0427, crates/sv-check/tests/plain_questions.rs).

questions.title: Input validation is enforced at a trusted service layer
questions.asks: Does the application enforce input validation on the server — a trusted service layer — and not only in the browser? Client-side validation improves usability and should be kept, but anyone can skip it by sending a request straight to the server, so it settles nothing on its own.
questions.plain: When someone types something into a form, does the server check it before using it, and not only the page in their browser (which anyone can skip)?
questions.whereMeans: the file where input validation happens on the server
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the app receives a form or an API request, and look at what happens to the values before they are used. If the only checks you find are in the browser — HTML attributes, JavaScript — that is the answer.

questions.title: Session tokens are verified by a trusted backend service
questions.asks: Does the application perform all session token verification using a trusted backend service, rather than believing something the browser sends about who is signed in?
questions.plain: When the app decides who is signed in, does the server check that against something it issued itself, rather than taking the browser's word for it?
questions.whereMeans: the file where the session is verified
questions.howToFindOut: Find the code that runs on every request and decides who is signed in. Check whether it verifies something the server issued, or simply believes a value from a cookie or header.

questions.title: Authorization rules are enforced at a trusted service layer
questions.asks: Does the application enforce its authorization rules at a trusted service layer — the server — rather than relying on controls an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as a hidden button or a disabled field in the browser? Hiding a link is not a rule: anyone can request the address directly.
questions.plain: When somebody tries to open a page or do something they are not allowed to, is it the server that stops them, or only a button that is hidden?
questions.whereMeans: the file where authorization is enforced
questions.howToFindOut: Take a page or an action only some people should reach, and find the code that stops everybody else. If the only thing you find is the button being hidden in the template, that is the answer.

questions.title: Only the fields that are needed are sent back
questions.asks: When the application returns a record, does it return only the required fields, rather than the whole object with fields the person should not see?
questions.plain: When the app sends a record to a page or another program, does it send only the parts that will be shown, and not the whole record with things that person should not see?
questions.whereMeans: the file that decides which fields are returned
questions.howToFindOut: Look at what an API returns for one record, or what a page sends to the browser, and compare it with what is shown. Anything extra in the response is being sent and simply not displayed.

questions.title: Input is decoded once, before it is checked
questions.asks: Is input decoded or unescaped into its final form exactly once, and before it is validated, rather than after? Decoding after the check lets something dangerous slip past a check that saw it encoded.
questions.plain: Where the app turns encoded text back into plain text (web addresses, base64, HTML), does it do that once, before checking the text, and never after?
questions.whereMeans: the file that decodes input
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the app decodes what it receives — URL decoding, base64, unescaping HTML — and check whether that happens before or after the values are checked. Twice is also worth looking for.

questions.title: Headers added by a load balancer cannot be faked
questions.asks: If a load balancer, proxy, or gateway sits in front of the application and adds header fields it relies on, can the application tell those apart from the same fields sent by a browser?
questions.plain: If something in front of the app (a load balancer, proxy, or gateway) adds information to each request that the app relies on, can the app tell that apart from the same information sent by a visitor?
questions.whereMeans: the file or configuration that handles those header fields
questions.howToFindOut: Find out what sits in front of the app and which header fields it adds. Then search the code for those names, and check whether the app can tell one the proxy set from one a browser sent.

questions.title: Everything in front of the app agrees where a request ends
questions.asks: Do all the components a request passes through — load balancers, firewalls, and the application server — agree on where one HTTP message ends and the next begins? When they disagree, somebody can hide a second request inside the first.
questions.plain: If a request passes through other machines before reaching the app (a load balancer, a firewall), do they all agree on where one request ends and the next begins?
questions.whereMeans: the configuration for the server or proxy in front of the app
questions.howToFindOut: Find what sits in front of the app — a load balancer, a reverse proxy, your host's edge. Check whether each one and the app agree on request size limits, chunked encoding, and duplicate headers. If you run nothing in front of the app, say so: that is the answer.
questions.whyNotChecked: The machines in front of the app, such as a load balancer, a reverse proxy, or your host's edge, are not in the app's folder, and StackVet runs the app on its own, with nothing in front of it. Sending the app a request built to be read two ways would test only the app's own server, and would say nothing about what is in front of it once the app is live.

questions.title: Access to individual fields is restricted
questions.asks: Where some fields of a record are more restricted than the record itself, does the application check permissions for those specific fields, both when read and when written?
questions.plain: Where some parts of a record are more private than the rest, does the app check who may see and who may change each of those parts, every time?
questions.whereMeans: the file that enforces field-level permissions
questions.howToFindOut: Take a record with a field not everybody should change, and find the code that saves it. Check whether it filters the fields it accepts, or takes whatever the request sends.

questions.title: Tokens go only where they are needed
questions.asks: Are access tokens sent only to the components that strictly need them, rather than handed to the browser when the server could hold them instead?
questions.plain: Are the app's access tokens kept only by the parts of the app that need them, rather than handed to the browser when the server could keep them?
questions.whereMeans: the file that handles tokens
questions.howToFindOut: Only where tokens are used. Find where the access token ends up: in the browser's storage, in a cookie, or kept on the server. Then list what actually needs it.

questions.title: Encryption choices can be changed later
questions.asks: Is the application designed so the algorithms, key lengths, and random number sources it uses for encryption and hashing can be replaced without rewriting it? Every algorithm in use now will eventually need replacing.
questions.plain: If one of the ways the app encrypts or scrambles data had to be swapped for a newer one, could that be done without rewriting the app?
questions.whereMeans: the file where the algorithms are chosen
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the app names an algorithm or a key length — hashing passwords, encrypting a field, signing a token. Check whether changing one would mean editing one place or many.

questions.title: Calls between the app's own backend components are authenticated
questions.asks: Where communications between backend application components — APIs, middleware, and data layers — do not carry the standard user session, is each call authenticated, so a caller has to prove who it is rather than merely being able to reach the address?
questions.plain: When parts of the app talk to each other (the app to its database, to a cache, to another of your services), does each one have to prove who it is, rather than being trusted because it can reach the address?
questions.whereMeans: the file where calls between services are authenticated
questions.howToFindOut: List the things the app talks to over a network that are not the person's browser: the database, a cache, another of your services. For each, find what proves who is calling.

questions.title: Accounts used between the app's own parts have the least privilege needed
questions.asks: Are communications between backend application components — local or operating system services, APIs, middleware, and data layers — performed with accounts assigned the least privileges necessary for each one, rather than one powerful account used everywhere because it is simpler?
questions.plain: Does each of those connections use an account allowed only what that part needs, rather than one powerful account used everywhere?
questions.whereMeans: the configuration that sets up those accounts
questions.howToFindOut: Look at the account the app uses for each of those connections and find out what it is allowed to do. A database account that can drop tables when the app only reads and writes rows is the answer.

questions.title: Sensitive data is not left in a cache
questions.asks: Does the application prevent sensitive data from being kept in caches it does not own — a load balancer, a content delivery network, or an application cache — or make sure anything kept there is protected?
questions.plain: Is private information kept out of the caches the app does not control (your host's edge, a content delivery network), or protected when it is stored there?
questions.whereMeans: the file or configuration that sets caching
questions.howToFindOut: List every cache a response passes through: your host's edge or CDN, a reverse proxy, the browser. Then look at what a private page sends back in Cache-Control. Anything sensitive without no-store is the answer to this one.

questions.title: The visitor's real address is passed along truthfully
questions.asks: If proxies or middleware sit in front of the application, do they pass the visitor's original IP address in a field the visitor cannot set themselves? Rate limits and logs are worth nothing if the address can be chosen by whoever is being limited.
questions.plain: If anything sits between visitors and the app, does it pass on each visitor's real internet address in a way the visitor cannot fake?
questions.whereMeans: the proxy configuration, or the file that reads the address
questions.howToFindOut: Find out whether anything sits between the visitor and the app. If so, check which header field carries the real address and whether the app would believe the same field sent by a visitor directly.

questions.title: Clocks agree, and times say which zone they are in
questions.asks: Do all the parts of the application that write logs keep their clocks synchronized, and do the timestamps use UTC or say which time zone they are in? Two logs with drifting clocks cannot be put in order after an incident.
questions.plain: Do all the parts of the app that keep logs have clocks that agree, and does every time they write say which time zone it is in?
questions.whereMeans: the logging configuration
questions.howToFindOut: Look at a few recent log lines from each part of the app and compare their timestamps. Check whether they say which time zone they are in, and whether two parts logging the same moment agree.

questions.title: Logs are sent somewhere separate
questions.asks: Are logs sent to a separate system, so that somebody who takes over the application cannot quietly delete the record of what they did?
questions.plain: Are the app's logs sent to a separate place, so someone who took over the app could not quietly delete them?
questions.whereMeans: the configuration that ships the logs
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the logs end up. If the answer is a file on the same machine the app runs on, then somebody who takes over the app can edit them, and this is not done.

questions.title: A change in several steps happens whole or not at all
questions.asks: When one business operation changes several records (an order and its stock, a transfer between two accounts, a booking and its payment), does the application use transactions so the operation either succeeds in its entirety or is rolled back to the previous correct state?
questions.plain: When one action changes several things at once (an order and the stock it takes, money leaving one account and arriving in another), is it set up so either all of the changes happen or none do, never half?
questions.whereMeans: the file that groups the changes into one transaction
questions.howToFindOut: Find the actions that change more than one record at once. For each, look for where the changes are grouped into one transaction (`with transaction.atomic()`, `db.transaction(...)`, `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`). Then ask what happens if the second change fails after the first succeeded: the first should be undone.

questions.title: How strongly someone signed in is checked from what the provider said
questions.asks: If the application uses a separate identity provider and expects a specific authentication strength, method, or recentness for some functions, does it verify this using the information returned by the provider (for OIDC, the ID Token's 'acr', 'amr', and 'auth_time' claims), and if the provider does not return it, is there a documented fallback that assumes the minimum strength authentication mechanism was used?
questions.plain: When people sign in through another service (Google, Microsoft, and the like), does the app ever need to know how they signed in there, for example with a second factor or within the last few minutes? If so, does it check what that service said, and if the service says nothing, does it assume the weakest sign-in?
questions.whereMeans: the file that reads what the sign-in provider returned
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the app reads what the provider sent back after sign-in. If it uses only the person's identifier, email, and name, and no part of the app needs a stronger or more recent sign-in, write that down: it is the answer. If some part does, check that it looks at `acr`, `amr`, or `auth_time`, and what it does when they are missing.

questions.title: Codes by phone or SMS go only to a confirmed number, beside a stronger way
questions.asks: If the app sends one-time passwords by phone call or SMS, is the phone number validated first, is a stronger method (such as an authenticator app's time-based codes) also offered, and are people told the security risks of phone and SMS codes?
questions.plain: If the app texts or phones people a sign-in code, does it check the number is really theirs first, does it also offer a safer way (an authenticator app), and does it tell people why text messages are the weaker choice?
questions.whereMeans: the file that sends sign-in codes by phone or SMS
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the app sends a text or makes a call (a Twilio, Vonage, or similar package, or the provider's settings). Then look at the sign-up or settings page where a phone number is added: is a code sent to it before it can be used?

questions.title: A second identity provider cannot sign someone in as another person
questions.asks: If the application supports multiple identity providers, is each user registered and identified by the identity provider's id together with the user's id at that provider, so the same user identifier from another supported provider cannot be used to spoof them?
questions.plain: If people can sign in through more than one service (Google and Microsoft, say), does the app remember which service each person came from, so someone with the same name or email at another service cannot sign in as them?
questions.whereMeans: the file that matches a provider's sign-in to a user record
questions.howToFindOut: Find the code that runs when a sign-in comes back from the provider, and see what it looks the user up by. If it is the email, or the provider's user id alone, without which provider it was, that is the problem this asks about. If the app has only one provider, write that down.

questions.title: Each SAML assertion is used only once
questions.asks: Does the application process each SAML assertion uniquely and use it only once within its validity period, refusing the same assertion a second time, to prevent replay attacks?
questions.plain: When someone signs in through SAML (common with company sign-in), does the app refuse the same sign-in message if it is sent to it a second time?
questions.whereMeans: the file or setting that records which SAML assertions were already used
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the app's SAML library is set up, and look in its settings or documentation for remembering assertion ids (often called replay protection or a message cache). Some libraries do it only when given somewhere to store them.

questions.title: A token proves the sign-in was strong or recent enough when that matters
questions.asks: Where the resource server requires a specific authentication strength, method, or recentness for an action, does it verify that the presented access token satisfies these constraints, for example using the OIDC acr, amr, and auth_time claims?
questions.plain: For an action that should need a recent sign-in, or a second step such as a code, does the app check the sign-in token says that really happened, rather than accepting any valid token?
questions.whereMeans: the file that checks the token's sign-in strength or time
questions.howToFindOut: List the actions that should need a fresh or stronger sign-in (changing a password, moving money). Then find the code that checks the token for those routes, and look for `acr`, `amr`, or `auth_time`. If nothing reads them, the token's age and strength are not checked.

questions.title: Clients that register themselves are checked, and people are warned
questions.asks: If the authorization server supports unauthenticated dynamic client registration, does it validate each new client's metadata, such as its registered addresses, make sure the user consents, and warn the user before an authorization request from an untrusted client application?
questions.plain: If any program can sign itself up as a client of the app's sign-in server without asking first, does the server check what it says about itself, and warn people before they approve one it does not know?
questions.whereMeans: the file or setting that controls client registration on the authorization server
questions.howToFindOut: Look in the authorization server's settings for dynamic client registration (often a `registration_endpoint` in its published metadata). If it is off, write that down; if it is on, check what the server does with a new client's addresses and what the person sees before approving it.

questions.title: People can revoke refresh tokens from the sign-in server's own pages
questions.asks: Can an authorized user revoke refresh tokens and reference access tokens through the authorization server's user interface, so a malicious client or a stolen token can be cut off?
questions.plain: Can a signed-in person, on the sign-in server's own pages, see what is still signed in on their behalf and switch it off, so a stolen token stops working?
questions.whereMeans: the page or file where a user revokes their tokens
questions.howToFindOut: Sign in as a test user and look through the account pages of the authorization server for a list of apps or sessions with a way to remove one. Then check that removing one really stops its token being accepted.

questions.title: The DTLS certificate's key is kept as the key policy says
questions.asks: Is the key for the media's Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate managed and protected as the documented policy for cryptographic keys says: where it is kept, who can read it, and when it is replaced?
questions.plain: For live audio or video, the connection is protected with a certificate whose secret key the app or its media server keeps: where is that key stored, who can read it, and is it handled the way the app's other keys are?
questions.whereMeans: the file or setting where the media server's DTLS key is made or kept
questions.howToFindOut: Find the media server's settings (mediasoup, LiveKit, Janus, or similar), or the hosted service's, and look for where the DTLS certificate and key come from. Many make a new one at each start, which is worth writing down; a fixed one is a file to protect like any other key.

questions.title: The media server uses approved DTLS cipher suites and SRTP profile
questions.asks: Is the media server configured to use and support only approved Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) cipher suites, and a secure protection profile for DTLS-SRTP, the extension that sets up keys for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol?
questions.plain: Is the media server for live audio and video set to use only the encryption choices that are currently approved, and not older weak ones kept for compatibility?
questions.whereMeans: the media server's setting that lists its DTLS cipher suites and SRTP profiles
questions.howToFindOut: Open the media server's configuration and look for its DTLS or SRTP settings: cipher suites, and SRTP protection profiles. Where none are set, the server's default list is the answer; write down which version and defaults it is.

questions.title: The media server checks SRTP authentication on every packet
questions.asks: Does the media server check Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) authentication, so that injected Real-time Transport Protocol packets cannot cause a denial of service or insert audio or video into a media stream?
questions.plain: Does the media server throw away any audio or video packet that fails its authentication check, so nobody can slip their own sound or picture into a call?
questions.whereMeans: the media server setting that turns SRTP authentication on or off
questions.howToFindOut: Look in the media server's configuration for anything that turns off SRTP authentication or allows unencrypted media for testing. Most servers check it unless told not to, so the thing to find is a setting that weakens it.

questions.title: Malformed SRTP packets do not stop the media server
questions.asks: Is the media server able to continue processing incoming media traffic when it encounters malformed Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) packets?
questions.plain: If the media server receives broken or garbled audio or video packets, does it drop them and carry on with everyone else's call, rather than stopping or crashing?
questions.whereMeans: the media server's version and its notes on malformed packets
questions.howToFindOut: Find which media server and version the app uses, then search its release notes and the advisory data for crashes on malformed packets. Running `sv report` with `--advisories` lists the known flaws in a version it can read.

questions.title: The signaling server keeps working during a flood, with rate limits
questions.asks: Is the signaling server able to continue processing legitimate incoming signaling messages during a flood attack, by rate limiting at the signaling level?
questions.plain: If someone floods the part of the app that sets up calls with messages, does it limit how many each sender can send, so real people can still start and join calls?
questions.whereMeans: the file that limits how many signaling messages each sender can send
questions.howToFindOut: Find the code that receives signaling messages (often a WebSocket handler for offers, answers, and candidates), and look for a limit on how many one connection or address may send. A rate-limit package on the web pages alone does not cover a WebSocket.

questions.title: Separate applications are on separate hostnames
questions.asks: Are separate applications hosted on different hostnames, so the same-origin policy keeps them apart: how documents or scripts loaded by one origin can interact with another's resources, and which cookies each can read?
questions.plain: If you run more than one application, does each have an address of its own (app.example.com and admin.example.com), rather than sharing one address in different folders, so a browser keeps their pages and cookies apart?
questions.whereMeans: the address each application is reached at
questions.howToFindOut: List every application you run on the same domain, and the address each is reached at. Two that share an address and differ only by path (example.com/app and example.com/blog) are what this asks about.

questions.title: Content sent to memcache is cleaned first
questions.asks: Does the application clean content before it is sent to memcache, so that a key or value cannot carry spaces, line breaks, or control characters that would inject a second memcache command, and keys are kept under memcache's 250-byte limit?
questions.plain: Where the app saves things in memcache (a fast store for temporary data), does it clean what people send before using it as a name or a value there, so they cannot sneak in a command of their own?
questions.whereMeans: the file that builds memcache keys from what people send
questions.howToFindOut: Start from the files StackVet lists as bringing in a memcache client. In each, look at what the keys are made from: a key built from a username, a search, or anything else a visitor typed should be hashed or have spaces and line breaks taken out first.

questions.title: Two parsers of the same kind of data read it the same way
questions.asks: Where different parsers in the application read the same data type (two JSON parsers, an XML parser in front of another, two URL parsers), do they parse it in a consistent way and with the same character encoding, so a value one reads one way cannot be read another way by the next?
questions.plain: Where two parts of the app (or the app and something in front of it) both read the same kind of data, a web address or a JSON message, do they always read it the same way, so a trick that fools one cannot slip past the other?
questions.whereMeans: the files where the same kind of data is parsed twice
questions.howToFindOut: Search the code for more than one library or function reading the same kind of data: two URL parsers, a JSON library and a hand-written reader, or a proxy's parsing in front of the app's. For each pair, write down which reads first and whether they were set up to agree, the character encoding included.

questions.title: High-value actions need a second person's approval
questions.asks: Do high-value business logic flows (large monetary transfers, contract approvals, access to classified information, safety overrides) require approval by more than one user before they happen, to prevent unauthorized or accidental actions?
questions.plain: For the actions in the app that would do the most harm if done by mistake or by the wrong person (a large payment, signing a contract), does a second person have to approve before it happens?
questions.whereMeans: the file that asks for a second approval before a high-value action
questions.howToFindOut: List the actions in the app that move money, sign something, or open restricted information. For each, try it as one test user and see whether it waits for another to approve. If the app has none of these, write that down.

questions.title: People are told before being sent to a site the app does not control
questions.asks: When the application redirects a user to a URL outside of its control, does it show a notification first, with an option to cancel the navigation?
questions.plain: When the app sends someone to another website, does it first show a page saying where they are going, with a way to go back instead?
questions.whereMeans: the file that redirects to an address outside the app
questions.howToFindOut: Search the code for redirects to full addresses (`redirect(`, `res.redirect(`, `Location:` with `https://`). For each one that can lead off the app's own site, check whether a page saying so comes first.

questions.title: The most sensitive requests carry a signature of their own
questions.asks: Are per-message digital signatures used, on top of transport protections such as HTTPS, for requests or transactions which are highly sensitive or which traverse a number of systems?
questions.plain: For the most sensitive messages the app sends or receives (a payment instruction, or one that passes through several systems), is each one signed on its own, so it is protected even if the secure connection is not the whole way?
questions.whereMeans: the file that signs or checks the signature on each message
questions.howToFindOut: List the requests that are most sensitive or that pass through more than one system, then search the code that sends and receives them for a signature (HMAC, JWS, a signed payload). HTTPS alone does not count here.

questions.title: Outgoing addresses and headers are kept short enough to be accepted
questions.asks: Where the application builds and sends requests, does it validate or otherwise limit what goes into the URI and HTTP header fields (such as Authorization or Cookie), so it never creates one too long to be accepted by the receiving component and so always answered with an error?
questions.plain: When the app builds a request to send somewhere (an address with things added to it, or a cookie), does it make sure it never gets too long for the other side to accept, so one long value cannot break every request after it?
questions.whereMeans: the file that builds outgoing requests from stored or typed values
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the app calls other services or sets cookies from values it stores or people type. Look for a limit on how long those values may be before they are put into an address or a header.

questions.title: Each person's uploads are held to a file count and a size quota
questions.asks: Is a file size quota and a maximum number of files per user enforced, so a single user cannot fill up the storage with too many files or excessively large files?
questions.plain: Is there a limit on how many files each person can upload, and on how much space their files may take altogether, so one person cannot fill up the app's storage?
questions.whereMeans: the file or setting that limits each person's number of files and total size
questions.howToFindOut: Look where uploads are saved for a check of how many files that person already has, or how much space they use. A limit on one file's size is not this; it is the total per person that matters.

questions.title: People are reminded in time to renew a way of signing in that expires
questions.asks: Where an authentication mechanism expires (a client certificate, a hardware token, a password with a fixed lifetime), are renewal instructions sent with enough time to be carried out before the old one expires, with automated reminders where needed?
questions.plain: If a way of signing in to the app runs out after a while (a certificate, or a key that must be renewed), does the app remind people early enough that they can renew it before it stops working?
questions.whereMeans: the file or job that sends renewal reminders
questions.howToFindOut: List each way of signing in that expires. For each, find out whether anything warns the person before it does (an email, a notice on sign-in) and how long before. If nothing expires, write that down.

questions.title: An administrator can start a reset without choosing or knowing the password
questions.asks: Can administrative users initiate the password reset process for a user without being able to change or choose that user's password, so an administrator never knows another user's password?
questions.plain: When someone asks an administrator for help with a forgotten password, can the administrator send them a reset link without ever choosing or seeing the new password themselves?
questions.whereMeans: the admin page or file that starts a password reset for another user
questions.howToFindOut: Sign in as an administrator and look at what you can do for another user's account. A button that sends that person a reset email is right; a field where you type their new password is what this asks about.

questions.title: Any way of signing in can be revoked when it is lost or stolen
questions.asks: Can any authentication factor (an authenticator app, a passkey, a physical security key, backup codes) be revoked in case of theft or other loss, by the person or by support, and replaced?
questions.plain: If someone loses their phone or a security key they use to sign in, can it be switched off so it no longer works, and a new one set up in its place?
questions.whereMeans: the file or page where a sign-in factor is removed
questions.howToFindOut: Sign in as a test user who has set up a second factor, and look in the account settings for a way to remove it. Then find out what support does for someone who has lost the device and cannot sign in at all.

questions.title: A fingerprint or face is only ever a second factor
questions.asks: Are biometric authentication mechanisms (a fingerprint, a face) only used as secondary factors, together with either something you have or something you know?
questions.plain: Where the app lets people sign in with a fingerprint or their face, is that always together with something else (their own device, or a password), never on its own?
questions.whereMeans: the file that accepts a biometric sign-in
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the app takes a fingerprint or face sign-in. A passkey unlocked by a fingerprint on the person's own device is the fingerprint plus the device, which is what this asks for; a face matched on a server with nothing else is not.

questions.title: The adaptive controls the documentation describes are built, at sign-in and during a session
questions.asks: Are the adaptive security controls based on a consumer's environmental and contextual attributes (time of day, location, IP address, device) implemented for authentication and authorization decisions as the application's documentation defines them, both when a new session starts and during an existing session?
questions.plain: If the app's notes say it treats a sign-in differently by time, place, address, or device, does the code really do that, both when someone signs in and later while they are still signed in?
questions.whereMeans: the file that applies the time, place, address, or device rules
questions.howToFindOut: Start from what the security notes say for V8.1.3 and V8.1.4. For each rule written there, find the code that applies it at sign-in, and check it is applied again during a session, not only once.

questions.title: A service asked on a person's behalf decides on that person's permissions
questions.asks: Is access to an object based on the originating subject's permissions, not on those of any intermediary or service acting on their behalf: when one service requests data from another for a consumer, does the second decide using the consumer's token, rather than a machine-to-machine token from the first?
questions.plain: When one part of the app, another program, or an AI asks for a record on someone's behalf, does the part holding the record check what that person may see, and not just trust the one asking?
questions.whereMeans: the file where a service checks whose permissions to use
questions.howToFindOut: Find each place a request reaches the app through something acting for a person: another of its services, a program with an API key, or the app's AI. Check whether the person's own token or id travels with it, and whether that is what decides access.

questions.title: The resource server refuses a stolen or replayed access token
questions.asks: Does the resource server prevent the use of stolen access tokens, or their replay by unauthorized parties, by requiring sender-constrained access tokens, through Mutual TLS for OAuth 2 or OAuth 2 Demonstration of Proof of Possession (DPoP)?
questions.plain: If someone copied an access token the app accepts, could they use it from their own computer? Or does the app's API insist each token is used only by the program it was given to?
questions.whereMeans: the file where the API checks that a token is bound to the client presenting it
questions.howToFindOut: Find the code that checks access tokens on the app's API, and look for a `DPoP` header being checked, or the token's `cnf` claim compared with the client certificate. If tokens are accepted on their signature and expiry alone, a copied one works.

questions.title: The authorization server issues only sender-bound access tokens
questions.asks: Does the authorization server issue only sender-constrained (Proof-of-Possession) access tokens, either certificate-bound access tokens using mutual TLS (mTLS) or DPoP-bound access tokens, and never plain bearer tokens?
questions.plain: Does the app's own sign-in server only ever hand out tokens tied to the program that asked for them, so a token on its own is useless to anyone else?
questions.whereMeans: the authorization server setting that requires DPoP or certificate-bound tokens
questions.howToFindOut: Look in the authorization server's settings, and in its published metadata (`dpop_signing_alg_values_supported`, `tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens`). Advertising support is not the same as requiring it: check that a client asking without DPoP or a certificate is refused.

questions.title: Authorization details from a server-side client cannot be tampered with
questions.asks: For a server-side client, does the authorization server ensure the authorization_details parameter value comes from the client backend and that the user has not tampered with it, for example by requiring pushed authorization requests (PAR) or JWT-secured authorization requests (JAR)?
questions.plain: When a program on a server asks the app's sign-in server for permission to do specific things, is that request sent straight from server to server (or signed), so the person in the browser cannot change what is asked for on the way?
questions.whereMeans: the authorization server setting that requires PAR or JAR
questions.howToFindOut: Look in the authorization server's settings for pushed authorization requests (PAR) or signed request objects (JAR), and whether they are required for server-side clients or only allowed. If `authorization_details` is not used at all, write that down.

questions.title: Every use of cryptography in the system is found by a discovery tool
questions.asks: Are cryptographic discovery mechanisms employed to identify all instances of cryptography in the system, including encryption, hashing, and signing operations, in the code, its libraries, and its servers?
questions.plain: Does anyone run a tool that finds every place the system scrambles, signs, or fingerprints data (in the app's code, the packages it uses, and its servers), so none is missed when something has to be replaced?
questions.whereMeans: the tool or report that lists every use of cryptography
questions.howToFindOut: Start from the cryptography list written for V11.1.2. Then find out whether a tool produced it (a code scanner, a bill of materials with cryptography in it, a server scan) or a person wrote it from memory. A list from memory misses what packages and servers do.

questions.title: Memory is encrypted while sensitive data is in use
questions.asks: Is full memory encryption in use, protecting sensitive data while it is in use, so that unauthorized users or processes cannot read it from memory?
questions.plain: Does the app run on computers whose memory is encrypted (often called confidential computing), so that even someone with access to the machine cannot read sensitive data while the app is working on it?
questions.whereMeans: the hosting setting or machine type that encrypts memory
questions.howToFindOut: Look at where the app is hosted and which kind of machine it runs on. Cloud providers name these as confidential VMs or confidential computing (AMD SEV, Intel TDX). If it is an ordinary machine, write that down: that is the answer.

questions.title: Only the data needed is decrypted, and only while it is needed
questions.asks: Does data minimization ensure that the minimal amount of data is exposed during processing, and that data is encrypted again immediately after use or as soon as feasible?
questions.plain: When the app has to unlock sensitive data to work on it, does it unlock only the parts it needs, and lock them again as soon as it is done?
questions.whereMeans: the file where sensitive data is decrypted for processing
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the app decrypts stored sensitive data. Check whether it decrypts only the fields that step needs, and whether the plain values are kept only for that step, not cached or left in a long-lived object.

questions.title: Keys stay inside a vault or hardware module that does the cryptography
questions.asks: Are all cryptographic operations performed using an isolated security module, such as a vault or hardware security module, so that key material is managed there and never exposed outside of the security module?
questions.plain: Are the app's most important keys kept in a locked-away service (a key vault or a security chip) that does the signing and unlocking itself, so the keys never reach the app's own memory or files?
questions.whereMeans: the file or setting that sends cryptography to the vault or hardware module
questions.howToFindOut: Find where the app signs or decrypts. If it reads a key from an environment variable or a file and uses it in its own code, the key leaves the module. If it calls a key service (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS, HashiCorp Vault's transit engine) to do the work, it does not.

questions.title: Secrets expire and are rotated as the documentation says
questions.asks: Are secrets configured to expire and be rotated as the application's documentation says they should be?
questions.plain: For each password or key the app uses, is it really set to run out and be replaced on the schedule the app's notes give, rather than only written down as a plan?
questions.whereMeans: the setting or job that expires and rotates each secret
questions.howToFindOut: Start from what the security notes say for V13.1.4. For each secret listed there, look at where it is kept for an expiry date or an automatic rotation, and check when it was last replaced.

questions.title: Only the sensitive data needed is returned, and it is masked
questions.asks: Does the application only return the minimum required sensitive data for its functionality, for example only some of the digits of a credit card number, and where the complete data is required, mask it in the user interface unless the user specifically views it?
questions.plain: When the app shows or sends sensitive details (a card number, an ID number), does it send only the part that is needed, such as the last four digits, and hide the rest on screen unless the person asks to see it?
questions.whereMeans: the file that decides how much of a sensitive value is returned
questions.howToFindOut: Open the pages and API responses that show sensitive details while signed in, and look at what arrives in the browser, not only what is shown. A full number sent and then hidden by the page is still returned.

questions.title: Outdated sensitive data is deleted on a schedule
questions.asks: Is sensitive information subject to data retention classification, so that outdated or unnecessary data is deleted automatically, on a defined schedule, or as the situation requires?
questions.plain: Does the app delete sensitive information it no longer needs (old accounts, old orders, old messages) on its own, on a schedule, rather than keeping everything for ever?
questions.whereMeans: the job or file that deletes data past its retention period
questions.howToFindOut: List the kinds of sensitive data the app keeps, and how long each should be kept. Then look for a scheduled job, or a database setting, that deletes each when its time is up. If nothing does, write that down.

questions.title: The risky parts of the app are walled off from the rest
questions.asks: Does the application implement additional protections, such as sandboxing, encapsulation, containerization, or network-level isolation, around the parts documented as containing dangerous functionality or using risky components, to delay and deter an attacker who compromises one part from pivoting elsewhere?
questions.plain: Are the parts of the app the notes call risky (the add-on packages and the dangerous features) kept apart from the rest, so someone who breaks in there cannot easily reach everything else?
questions.whereMeans: the setting or file that isolates the risky parts
questions.howToFindOut: Start from what the security notes say for V15.1.4 and V15.1.5. For each part listed, find out whether it runs in a container, process, or sandbox of its own with only the access it needs. If it runs inside the main app with all its access, write that down.

questions.title: Thread pools and queues give every task a fair turn
questions.asks: Do resource allocation policies prevent thread starvation by ensuring fair access to resources, for example through thread pools, so that lower-priority threads can proceed within a reasonable time?
questions.plain: When the app is busy, does every job eventually get its turn, or can a flood of one kind of work keep the rest waiting for ever?
questions.whereMeans: the file or setting that sizes the worker pools and queues
questions.howToFindOut: Find the app's worker and queue settings (the web server's worker count, a task queue's concurrency, a thread pool's size). Check that slow or low-priority work has a pool or queue of its own, or a time limit, so it cannot hold every worker.

questions.title: The media server keeps working during an SRTP flood from real users
questions.asks: Is the media server able to continue processing incoming media traffic during a flood of Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) packets from legitimate users?
questions.plain: If many real callers send a lot of audio and video at once, does the media server keep carrying everyone's calls, rather than falling over?
questions.whereMeans: the media server's limits and its load-test results
questions.howToFindOut: Find the media server's settings for how many streams and how much traffic each connection may send, and ask whether it has been load-tested at more than the busiest expected day. A hosted service's published limits are the answer for one.

questions.title: Recording keeps working during an SRTP flood from real users
questions.asks: Are the audio or video recording mechanisms associated with the media server able to continue processing incoming media traffic during a flood of SRTP packets from legitimate users?
questions.plain: If the app records calls, does recording keep working when many people send a lot of audio and video at once, rather than stopping or dropping parts of calls?
questions.whereMeans: the recording service's limits and its load-test results
questions.howToFindOut: Find what records calls (part of the media server, or a separate service), and look at its limits on how many streams it records at once. If the app does not record calls, write that down.

questions.title: The DTLS certificate is checked against the SDP fingerprint
questions.asks: Is the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate checked against the Session Description Protocol (SDP) fingerprint attribute, with the media stream terminated if the check fails, to ensure the authenticity of the media stream?
questions.plain: When a call starts, does the media server check that the other side's encryption certificate matches the one announced when the call was set up, and hang up if it does not?
questions.whereMeans: the media server setting that checks the certificate's fingerprint
questions.howToFindOut: Media libraries check this unless told not to, so look in the media server's settings for anything that turns the fingerprint check off or ignores a mismatch, often an option meant for testing.
